topic: I'm thinking about hiring my first employee but I'm nervous about the fixed costs. How do I know if I'm ready?

transcript.text: Honestly, that’s exactly where I am — I’m basically the only one behind the bar, and I’m covering opening and closing by myself. I’m afraid that payroll and payroll tax will eat up any margin I’ve got. What should I be looking at in my numbers before I’m really ready to add that fixed cost?

### Bottom‑line checklist — what you need to crunch before you hire a second bartender

| **Cost item** | **How to calculate it** | **Typical range for a bar** |
|---------------|------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **Base wages** | Multiply the hourly rate you plan to pay by the number of hours you’ll schedule per week, then × 52. Example: $15 hr × 30 hrs × 52 = $23,400 annual. | $12‑$20 / hr (varies by market) |
| **FICA (Social Security + Medicare)** | 6.2 % of wages up to the $2024 Social‑Security ceiling ($$) + 1.45 % of **all** wages.  Total employer side = **7.65 %** of payroll. | 7.65 % of payroll |
| **Federal Unemployment (FUTA)** | 0.6 % of the first $7,000 per employee (if you qualify for the maximum credit).  = $42 per employee per year. | ≤ $42 per employee |
| **State Unemployment (SUTA)** | Varies by state; most states sit between 1 %‑3 % of the first $7‑$15 k of wages.  Look up your state’s “new employer” rate. | Roughly 1‑3 % of payroll |
| **Workers‑comp insurance** | Premiums are a % of payroll set by your state & classification code (usually 0.5 %‑2 %).  Get a quote from your carrier. | 0.5‑2 % of payroll |
| **Payroll service fee** | Fixed monthly fee ($20‑$50) + optional per‑paycheck charge ($1‑$2).  Many providers (Gusto, QuickBooks, Square Payroll) have a “starter” plan for ≤ 5 employees. | $20‑$50 / mo |
| **Other benefits (if any)** | Any health stipend, retirement match, or paid time‑off.  Add them as a % of wages. | Variable |

> **Quick formula**  
> **Total labor cost** = Base wages × (1 + 0.0765 + SUTA% + Workers‑comp% + Benefits%) + FUTA + Payroll‑service fee  

> **Example (Texas, 2024)** – hiring one part‑timer at $15 hr, 30 hrs / wk:  
> • Base = $23,400  
> • FICA = $23,400 × 7.65 % = $1,788  
> • FUTA = $42  
> • SUTA (TX new‑employer 2.7 % of first $9,000) ≈ $243  
> • Workers‑comp (0.9 % of payroll) ≈ $211  
> • Payroll service = $30 / mo × 12 = $360  
> **Total annual cost** ≈ **$26,044** → **≈ 111 % of base wages** (i.e., a 11 % uplift).

---

## 1. Run a **labor‑cost‑percentage test**

1. **Pull your latest 12‑month sales data** (total receipts).  
2. **Calculate Current Labor %** = (Your own wages + your share of payroll taxes) ÷ Total sales.  
3. **Target industry benchmark** for a full‑service bar is **30‑35 %** of sales.  

If you’re already at, say, 28 % with just you, adding a second bartender who costs $26 k a year will push you to ~38 %, which signals a margin squeeze unless you can boost sales or shift scheduling.

---

## 2. Ask yourself these **data‑driven questions** before committing:

| Question | Why it matters | How to answer it |
|----------|----------------|------------------|
| **What’s the average ticket per cover?** | Determines how many extra drinks you need to sell to cover the new labor cost. | Divide total sales by total covers for the past 3 months. |
| **What are your peak‑hour gaps?** | If you’re losing sales because you can’t stay open longer, an extra set of hands can unlock revenue. | Map hourly sales; spot windows where you’re “closed” but demand exists. |
| **Can you restructure shifts to keep the new hire part‑time?** | Part‑time wages → lower payroll tax (no overtime, fewer benefits). | Draft a schedule that caps the new hire at ≤ 30 hrs / wk. |
| **Is there a qualified 1099 contractor option?** | Independent‑contractor status eliminates FICA/FUTA/SUTA, but misclassification risks heavy penalties. | Verify state rules (many states require “employee” status for bar staff who work regular hours under your direction). |
| **Do you have cash flow to cover the first 2‑3 months of payroll before sales bump in?** | Payroll is a fixed out‑flow; you need a buffer. | Keep a reserve equal to 2 × monthly labor cost (≈ $4 k‑$5 k in the example). |

---

## 3. Tools to get the numbers instantly

1. **Free payroll calculator** – Gusto’s “Payroll Tax Calculator” (enter state, wage, hours).  
2. **Industry labor‑cost benchmark** – The National Restaurant Association’s “Restaurant Industry Operations Report” (2024) shows average labor % by restaurant type.  
3. **State SUTA rate lookup** – Your state labor department’s website (e.g., `www.calworkforce.org` for CA, `www.tdlr.texas.gov` for TX).  

---

## 4. Next steps you can take **today**

| Action | How to do it | Time estimate |
|--------|--------------|---------------|
| **Pull the last 12 months of POS data** and compute total sales & average ticket. | Export from your POS (Square, Toast, Lightspeed). | 15 min |
| **Draft a simple labor‑cost model** in a spreadsheet using the formula above. | Plug in 2 scenarios: (a) keep solo, (b) add part‑timer at $15 hr. | 30 min |
| **Get a workers‑comp quote** from your current insurer (or a quick online quote). | Call or use an online portal; mention “bar/tavern – bartender classification”. | 10 min |
| **Check your state’s SUTA rate** for a new employer. | Search “[Your State] new employer unemployment tax rate 2024”. | 5 min |
| **Run the labor‑% test** and see where you land vs the 30‑35 % benchmark. | Use the spreadsheet to calculate % of sales. | 5 min |
| **Decide on hire type** – full‑time, part‑time, or 1099 (if legally viable). | Review the answers to the questions above. | 10 min |

---

### TL;DR

1. **Calculate total labor cost**: Base wages × 1.0765 + SUTA + workers’ comp + payroll‑service + FUTA.  
2. **Compare that total to your sales** – aim for ≤ 35 % of revenue.  
3. **Validate the business case** by confirming you have enough uncovered demand (peak hours, ticket size) to absorb the extra cost.  
4. **Gather the concrete numbers** (state SUTA rate, workers‑comp quote, current sales) before you post a job description.

Once you have those figures, you’ll see whether a second bartender is a margin eater or a profit driver. Let me know what your current monthly sales and wage plan look like, and I can help you run the exact numbers for your bar.

transcript.text: Okay, that helps. I can definitely pull the last 12 months of POS sales, but I’m not sure how to count my own wage since I don’t really give myself a formal paycheck. I’m doing maybe 55–60 hours a week and sales are around $32k/month—would you still load a wage on me for that labor-percentage test, or should I just focus on what the new hire needs to sell to cover their cost?

### 1. Treat Your Own Labor Like a “Salary” for the Test  

Even if you don’t draw a formal paycheck, the **owner‑labor cost matters** because it’s real time you could be doing something else (marketing, ordering, menu development, etc.). The labor‑percentage benchmark (30‑35 % of sales) is calculated on *total* labor—owner + employees.

**How to estimate it quickly**

| Step | What to do | Reason |
|------|------------|--------|
| **Pick a market‑rate hourly pay** for a bartender of your skill level in your city. | Look up “bartender hourly wage [Your City] 2024” (e.g., $15‑$18 / hr in many mid‑size markets). | This gives you a neutral baseline; you can adjust later if you feel you’re under‑/over‑paying yourself. |
| **Multiply by your actual hours** (55‑60 hrs / wk). | 58 hrs × $16 ≈ $928 / wk → $928 × 52 ≈ $48,200 annual. | That’s the “owner‑labor base” you’ll plug into the labor % calculation. |
| **Add the statutory employer taxes** (7.65 % FICA + any state SUTA + workers‑comp). | $48,200 × 0.0765 ≈ $3,690. | This keeps the test realistic. |

**Result:** Roughly **$52 k – $55 k** of annual labor cost for you alone.

---

### 2. Run the Labor‑% Test With Your Owner Cost Included  

1. **Annual sales**: $32k × 12 = $384,000.  
2. **Current labor (owner only)**: ≈ $52,000 → **Labor % = $52k / $384k ≈ 13.5 %**.  

That’s comfortably below the 30‑35 % target, which means you have “headroom” for at least one more employee before you hit the benchmark.

---

### 3. How Much Must the New Bartender Contribute?

Use the *target labor %* to back‑solve the required sales contribution.

**Target total labor %** (pick a conservative 32 %):  

\[
\text{Maximum allowable total labor cost} = 0.32 \times \$384{,}000 \approx \$122{,}880.
\]

**Subtract your existing labor cost** (≈ $52 k):  

\[
\$122{,}880 - \$52{,}000 \approx \$70{,}880 \text{ “room” for new hires.}
\]

**Annual cost of a part‑time bartender (30 hrs / wk, $15 / hr)**  

| Item | Calculation | Cost |
|------|-------------|------|
| Base wages | $15 × 30 hrs × 52 wk | $23,400 |
| Employer FICA (7.65 %) | $23,400 × 0.0765 | $1,788 |
| FUTA (max) | $42 | $42 |
| SUTA (example 2 % of $7k) | $140 | $140 |
| Workers‑comp (0.9 % of payroll) | $211 | $211 |
| Payroll service (Gusto starter) | $30 × 12 | $360 |
| **Total** | — | **≈ $26,000** |

**Bottom line:**  
- **Cost to you:** ~ $26 k / yr.  
- **Room available:** ~$70 k / yr.  

**Sales needed to cover the hire** = $26 k ÷ $384 k ≈ **6.8 %** of your monthly sales. In dollar terms:

\[
\$32{,}000 \times 0.068 \approx \$2{,}176 \text{ extra sales each month}.
\]

If a single bartender can generate an additional **$2.2 k / month** (e.g., 50 extra covers at $44 average ticket, or 30 higher‑margin cocktails), the hire pays for itself and you stay under the 32 % labor ceiling.

---

### 4. Action Checklist Right Now

| Action | How to do it | Time |
|--------|--------------|------|
| **Assign yourself a market‑rate hourly wage** (e.g., $16 / hr). | Google “bartender hourly wage [Your City] 2024”. | 5 min |
| **Calculate your “owner labor cost”** (hours × rate × 52 + 7.65 % tax). | Use a quick spreadsheet or calculator. | 5 min |
| **Plug that number into the labor‑% formula** (owner labor ÷ annual sales). | Verify you’re below 30‑35 %. | 5 min |
| **Estimate the new hire’s total cost** with the table above (adjust rate/hours to your real plan). | Use the same spreadsheet. | 10 min |
| **Determine the sales gap**: required extra monthly sales = new‑hire cost ÷ 12 ÷ (average ticket). | If your average ticket is $44, you need ~50 extra covers/month. | 10 min |
| **Validate demand**: Look at your POS hourly sales for the next‑most‑busy shift. | See if you can realistically add those extra covers. | 15 min |
| **Create a hiring budget** (wage, taxes, workers‑comp, payroll service) and put it into your monthly cash‑flow forecast. | Add a line item “Bartender – Payroll”. | 10 min |

---

### 5. Quick Decision Tree

| Situation | What to do |
|-----------|------------|
| **Owner labor % < 20 %** *and* you have clear peak‑hour demand → **Hire** a part‑time bartender. |
| **Owner labor % ≈ 30 %** *or* sales are flat → **Delay** or look for a **revenues‑boosting fix** (happy hour, cocktail menu redesign) before adding payroll. |
| **Owner labor % > 35 %** *or* cash‑flow tight → **Do not hire** until you can either increase sales or cut other variable costs (e.g., reduce overtime, renegotiate liquor contracts). |

---

**Bottom line:**  
- Put a **realistic market wage on yourself** and include the employer payroll taxes—this gives you a true labor % today.  
- With your current numbers you have roughly **$70 k** of labor “room,” which comfortably covers a part‑time bartender costing ≈ $26 k / yr.  
- Translate that into **$2.2 k extra sales each month** and test whether your busy periods can produce that volume. If yes, go ahead; if not, focus first on increasing ticket size or extending hours before you add payroll.

Let me know what market wage you settle on for yourself and whether you plan a part‑time or full‑time schedule for the new bartender—I can then fine‑tune the exact sales‑gap calculation for your bar.
